dropped.claim: Any quiet verdict that is not not_on_untappd is counted as wontfix, including the matcher_bug verdicts that guard 3 now produces by degrading not_on_untappd.

results.claim: The model-authored `issue.body` is placed before the rendered scope block, while `BLOCK_RE` takes the first match, so a ```triage-scope fence in the body supplies the scope that is parsed next run.
results.whyItBreaks: The model writes `body`, and if it contains a fenced ```triage-scope block (for example one copied from an open issue it saw in the prompt), `parseScopeBlock` returns that block instead of the real one appended by `renderScopeBlock`. The scope hijack the PR fixed for `contains` values is still open through the body. The PR's claim that the parser never sees model prose does not hold.
results.evidence: Line 318 builds `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)}` with the model-authored body first, so if the parser takes the first match (as the finding says of BLOCK_RE, which is outside this file), a fence in the body overrides the real scope, contradicting the comment above it that the parser sees only our own output.

results.quote:
if (!allowedKeys.has(verdict.new_issue_key!)) { skipped++; continue; }
      pushInto(byKey, verdict.new_issue_key!, verdict);
results.claim: Verdicts attached to a new issue are never checked against that issue's proposed scope, so guard 2 applies only to existing issues.
results.whyItBreaks: The model can propose a new issue with scope `candidates_count > 0` and attach a verdict whose row has `candidates_count = 0`. That row contradicts the scope but is still filed against the new issue, which is the same misroute guard 2 exists to stop.
results.evidence: The new-issue branch only checks `allowedKeys.has(...)` before `pushInto(byKey, ...)` and never calls `rowSatisfiesScope` against the cappedIssues entry's `scope`, while the existing-issue branch does.

results.claim: The saturation check uses a count read before the run and is not incremented as verdicts are attached within the same batch.
results.whyItBreaks: An issue with 11 post-creation rows passes the check for every verdict in a batch of up to 50 rows. All of them attach in one comment, taking the issue far past MAX_ROWS_PER_ISSUE=12 and recreating the pile the guard is meant to prevent.
results.evidence: Guard 4 compares the static `target.postCreationRows` from `byNumber` with MAX_ROWS_PER_ISSUE, and the loop never increments it or counts `byIssue.get(n).length`, so one batch can push an issue at 11 rows well past 12.

results.claim: The tool schema leaves `col` and `op` as free strings, but the zod `ScopeSchema` rejects any unknown column or operator, so one malformed scope fails parsing of the entire analysis.
results.whyItBreaks: If the model emits a `where` term with an unsupported col/op, or `value: null` on a `contains` or numeric term, `AnalysisSchema.parse` fails for the whole payload. All verdicts for the batch are lost, not just the one bad proposed issue. Guard 1 never gets to drop it individually.
results.evidence: AnalysisSchema embeds `scope: ScopeSchema` inside the `new_issues` array, so any single scope rejection fails the whole `parse`; the tool schema types `col` and `op` as plain `{ type: 'string' }` and does not constrain them, while the file's own comments say the zod side should be lenient so a bad item does not fail the whole batch.

dropped.claim: Quiet verdicts that guard 3 degrades from not_on_untappd to matcher_bug are counted as wontfix in the outcome and digest line.

results.claim: The saturation guard checks only rows already persisted and does not count verdicts attached to the same issue earlier in this run.
results.whyItBreaks: With an issue at postCreationRows=0 and a batch of up to 50 orphans all pointing at it and passing the scope check, every one is attached in a single comment. That exceeds MAX_ROWS_PER_ISSUE=12 in one run, which is the pile-up the guard exists to stop.
results.evidence: The Guard 4 check `target.postCreationRows >= MAX_ROWS_PER_ISSUE` reads only the persisted count, while rows pushed into `byIssue` earlier in the same loop are never counted, so one run can push an issue past 12.

results.claim: Verdicts routed to a new_issue_key are never checked against that new issue's own scope.
results.whyItBreaks: A model can propose a new issue scoped candidates_count > 0 and file a candidates_count = 0 row against it. The issue is created already contradicting its attached row, and the row gets issue_number set. Guard 2's contradiction check only runs for existing-issue attachments.
results.evidence: The new_issue_key `else` branch only checks `allowedKeys.has(...)` before `pushInto(byKey, ...)`, and `rowSatisfiesScope` is called only in the `hasIssue` branch, so a row is never checked against the scope of the new issue it is filed under.

results.claim: The scope parser takes the first fenced triage-scope block in the whole issue body, and the body prefix is model-authored free text.
results.whyItBreaks: createIssue sends `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(...)}`. If the model-written body contains its own ```triage-scope fence (for example copied from a scraped name or an injected instruction), BLOCK_RE matches that block first. The next run then parses a different valid-looking scope, which the PR says it eliminates only for the contains-value case.
results.evidence: BLOCK_RE has no `g` flag and parseScopeBlock uses `BLOCK_RE.exec(body)` on the whole body, so it takes the first ```triage-scope fence; renderScopeBlock only sanitizes backticks in its own output, so a fence in any text placed before the rendered block would be parsed instead of the real one.

results.claim: A strict, required scope is now embedded in AnalysisSchema, while the tool schema types `col` and `op` as free strings, so one bad scope term can fail the whole analysis.
results.whyItBreaks: The tool schema allows any string for col/op. If the model emits an unknown column or operator in one new_issue's scope (e.g. col 'brewery' with op '='), AnalysisSchema.parse presumably rejects the entire payload, including every valid verdict. The previous behaviour was lenient parsing. The parse call site is not shown, so this is inferred.
results.evidence: Whether a bad col/op rejects the whole payload depends on ScopeSchema in triage-scope.ts and on the parse call site, neither of which is in this file, and the finding itself says the claim is inferred.

results.claim: The string comparison between GitHub's created_at ('...:00Z') and the stored reviewed_at ('...:00.000Z') mis-orders timestamps within the same second.
results.whyItBreaks: Comparing 'Z' (0x5A) against '.' (0x2E) at the fractional-seconds position makes the GitHub created_at sort after a reviewed_at in the same second. A row attached in the same second as issue creation is therefore not counted. This is a minor undercount.
results.evidence: The comparison `reviewed_at > ?` in countRowsForIssue only misorders if the caller passes a second-precision GitHub created_at and stores millisecond ISO strings, neither of which is visible in this file, and the claim itself calls the effect a minor undercount.

results.quote:
if (scope.beer_ids.length > 0) return true;
  return scope.where.some((t) => t.col !== 'review_class');
results.claim: isLegalScope accepts any scope with a non-empty beer_ids, even when `where` is only a review_class term, but rowSatisfiesScope ORs beer_ids with where.
results.whyItBreaks: The model submits {beer_ids:[1], where:[{col:'review_class',op:'=',value:'matcher_bug'}]}. Guard 1 passes it because beer_ids is non-empty. The scope still matches every future matcher_bug row through the where clause, so it re-creates the whole-class dumping ground that guard 1 exists to stop.
results.evidence: isLegalScope returns true on non-empty beer_ids without inspecting where, while rowSatisfiesScope falls through to scope.where.every(...) for rows outside the cohort, so {beer_ids:[1], where:[review_class=matcher_bug]} matches every matcher_bug row, which is the class-only shape the comment says must not qualify.

results.claim: The model-authored issue.body is placed before the rendered scope block, and BLOCK_RE takes the first match, so a fence in the body can hijack the scope parse.
results.whyItBreaks: issue.body is free model text derived from scraped shop data. If it contains a ```triage-scope block with valid JSON, parseScopeBlock returns that scope instead of the real one. This is the same silent-hijack class that was fixed for `contains` values, but through a path the fix does not cover.
results.evidence: Line 318 only concatenates `${issue.body}` ahead of `renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)`; whether a fence in the body is parsed first depends on BLOCK_RE and `parseScopeBlock` in domain/triage-scope.ts, which this file does not show, so the claim cannot be settled here.

results.claim: The saturation check uses a static pre-run row count and is never incremented as verdicts are attached within the same run.
results.whyItBreaks: An issue with 11 post-creation rows is still unsaturated. A batch of up to 50 orphans can then attach all of them in one comment, taking the issue far past MAX_ROWS_PER_ISSUE. Saturation only takes effect on the next run.
results.evidence: The guard reads target.postCreationRows, which is never updated inside the loop, and pushInto(byIssue, ...) appends unbounded verdicts, so an issue at 11 rows can receive the whole batch in one run.

results.quote:
if (!allowedKeys.has(verdict.new_issue_key!)) { skipped++; continue; }
      pushInto(byKey, verdict.new_issue_key!, verdict);
results.claim: Verdicts routed to a new issue are never checked against that new issue's own scope, so guard 2 applies only to existing issues.
results.whyItBreaks: The model proposes a new issue scoped candidates_count > 0 or beer_ids [1,2] but attaches beer 7 with candidates_count 0 to it. The row is attached anyway. The issue is then born holding a row that contradicts its own scope, which is the contradiction guard 2 is meant to prevent.
results.evidence: The new-issue branch only checks allowedKeys.has(key) and never calls rowSatisfiesScope against the proposed entry's scope, even though cappedIssues carry a scope and the existing-issue branch enforces Guard 2.

results.claim: Absence is treated as proven when either the brewery probe or the name probe is empty, even if the other probe returned hits.
results.whyItBreaks: If the brewery-alone probe returned '' (brewery label wrong or noisy) but the name-alone probe found the beer under another brewery, not_on_untappd survives as terminal. The prompt itself says that case is a brewery-label problem. The guard's own comment says hits from other breweries are not absence evidence, but this OR admits them.
results.evidence: `probe?.brewery === '' || probe?.name === ''` accepts either empty probe as proof, while the comment above says hits from OTHER breweries read as absence 4 times out of 11, which a name-only empty vs brewery-empty split can still admit.

results.claim: A strict ScopeSchema inside the otherwise lenient AnalysisSchema means one bad scope term fails parsing of the whole analysis.
results.whyItBreaks: The tool schema types col and op as free strings with no enum. If the model emits an unknown col or op, or a null value on a numeric term, zod rejects the whole payload, and every verdict in the batch of up to 50 is lost. The failure is likely non-transient, so the day is consumed with an error instead of the one proposal being dropped.
results.evidence: `scope: ScopeSchema` sits inside the `new_issues` array of `AnalysisSchema` with no `.catch`/`safeParse` wrapper, while `ANALYSIS_TOOL_SCHEMA` types `col` and `op` as plain `{ type: 'string' }` with no enum, so any term ScopeSchema rejects fails the whole payload despite the file's stated goal of not failing the whole batch; ScopeSchema's own strictness lives in triage-scope.ts and was not visible, so this rests on that assumption.
